notes: "The sage did not show the way down." reads slightly oddly ('show the way' suggests guiding); 'The sage did not tell him how to go down.' is more natural.
"The horse went over many lands." could be 'over many countries' for a beginner; "His father held him close." could be 'His father hugged him.'
The A1 text never says the second king kept the horse, so "Bring the horse outside" arrives a little abruptly; optional: add 'The king kept the horse too.' after 'He took the princess from the sage.'
"Three sages came from far countries" / "to a far country": 'faraway countries' / 'a faraway country' is more idiomatic.
"There, a king took the princess to his palace. He put the sage in a dark room." skips why; optional: 'The princess told him the truth, so he put the sage in a dark room.'
The king's taking of the ebony horse is implied but never stated before the prince asks for it; optional: '...threw the sage into prison and kept the ebony horse.'
In the Sana escape the horse is on the roof and the soldiers gather in the courtyard; 'the prince simply climbed onto his horse' could add 'went up to the roof' for clarity, but it is not confusing.
"if it truly flew as the sage claimed" sits oddly after the king has just watched it fly; it works as a pretext since the king is 'seizing on a way to delay', so this is taste only.
"tore up every letter the king sent" is a slightly odd detail for someone living in the same palace, but harmless.

summary: A faithful, child-safe retelling of the Arabian Nights tale (three sages' gifts, the peg trick, Sana, the sage's abduction, feigned madness, the doctor ruse, marriage) with consistent events across all five levels. Grammar fits each level's limits, quiz keys are correct and unambiguous, and the A1 text is understandable with the glossed words. Only minor stylistic and small-gap notes remain.
